rationale: Use one Ridge model for all drugs as before, but pick each drug's own penalty with efficient leave-one-out GCV (RidgeCV with alpha_per_target) instead of a fixed alpha=5000. Expression predicts some drugs well (targeted oncology agents) and others hardly at all (many non-oncology repurposing compounds), so the strong-signal drugs should get less shrinkage and the weak, noisy ones more.

A large share of drug sensitivity in PRISM follows tissue lineage. With alpha=5000, the ridge model shrinks those lineage signals heavily when they are spread over thousands of genes. This change first fits a per-drug lineage mean from the training lines, pulled toward the drug's overall mean in proportion to how few lines that lineage has (shrinkage). The expression ridge then models only what is left over after that lineage mean, and the two parts are added at prediction time.

Many PRISM drugs carry only weak, noisy signal on their own, but drug responses are strongly correlated with each other (general cytotoxicity, shared mechanism of action, lineage axes). This change keeps the same ridge but makes it reduced-rank: the ridge predictions are projected onto the top-k drug-response components of the fitted values, so weak drugs borrow strength from shared response axes. k is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold.

The reduced-rank step runs the SVD on raw AUC values, so the shared response axes are dominated by the drugs with the largest AUC variance. This change z-scores each drug's AUC (using training-fold mean and SD, with missing values filled as 0) before the ridge and the projection, then transforms the predictions back. Every drug then counts equally when the shared axes are built. The ridge itself is fit separately per drug with one alpha, so per-drug Pearson is unchanged before projection and only the shared-axis estimate changes.

The reduced-rank projection already removes noise along weak drug-response directions, so the fixed ridge penalty (alpha=5000, chosen without the projection) is probably too strong for the combined model. This change picks one global alpha together with the rank k by grouped inner CV. One eigendecomposition of the line-by-line kernel per fold makes every alpha almost free to evaluate. Round 1 tuned a separate alpha per drug with leave-one-out GCV and lost; this keeps one shared alpha and uses grouped CV instead.

For targeted drugs, the expression of the drug's own target gene (e.g. EGFR or ERBB2 inhibitors, BCL2 for venetoclax) is often the strongest predictor of response. With alpha=5000 spread over 5,000 genes, that single-gene signal is almost entirely shrunk away, and the shared low-rank projection then removes what little remains. This change fits a second ridge for each drug in which its annotated target genes get a much weaker penalty (their kernel is up-weighted by w²). The drug-specific difference from the base prediction is added after the reduced-rank projection. The weight w² is chosen jointly with k by grouped inner CV, and w²=0 reproduces the current model exactly.

This extends the kept target-gene term (round 6) with STRING network propagation. Many PRISM drug targets are barely expressed, or their effect runs through pathway partners: for example, the expression of BCL2-family partners or downstream kinases. So for each drug, the 20 highest-confidence STRING neighbours of its annotated targets are added as a second weakly penalised kernel block, with a relative weight β. β is chosen jointly with k and w² by grouped inner CV, and β=0 gives back the current model exactly.

Pathway-based kernels were the main ingredient of the DREAM drug-sensitivity winner (Bayesian multitask MKL). This change adds a block of Hallmark and Reactome pathway activity scores (the mean of the train-standardized member genes) to the gene features, with relative weight γ. That pushes the ridge, the shared low-rank axes and the target deltas toward coordinated pathway programmes rather than single-gene noise. γ is chosen jointly with k and w² by grouped inner CV, and γ=0 recovers the current model exactly.

All three parts of the current model (ridge, low-rank axes, target deltas) are linear. A Gaussian RBF kernel on the 5,000-gene profile adds similarity-based transfer: lines with globally similar transcriptomes (same lineage or subtype, e.g. haematopoietic, melanocytic) get similar responses. It can also pick up non-additive or threshold effects. This change adds an RBF block (median-distance bandwidth, centered on the training lines, with its trace matched to the linear kernel) to the existing kernel with weight η. η is chosen jointly with γ, k and w² by grouped inner CV, and η=0 gives back the current model exactly.

Much of PRISM drug sensitivity follows tissue lineage. The RBF and pathway blocks only pick this up indirectly through expression similarity, and round 2's separate lineage-mean model lost. This change adds a lineage kernel block instead: one-hot OncotreeLineage plus OncotreePrimaryDisease from `meta_train`/`meta_test`, centered and scaled to the same trace as the linear kernel, then added to the existing kernel with weight λ. So lineage enters the same jointly regularized multi-task ridge, the low-rank axes and the target deltas. λ is chosen by grouped inner CV in a second stage at the best (γ, η) to keep within the time limit, and λ=0 gives back the current model exactly.

Some drug × line AUCs in the training matrix are unmeasured. The model currently fills these with 0 in z-space, so it treats them as observed average responses. That biases each drug's ridge fit and the SVD that defines the shared response axes. This change fills the gaps from a low-rank reconstruction of the training response matrix (hard-impute SVD), using the line's measured responses to correlated drugs. The imputation rank r ∈ {3, 8, 20} is chosen by grouped inner CV in a second stage, at the best (γ, η), against observed values only. r=0 (the current zero-fill) stays a candidate, so the current model is recovered if imputation doesn't help.

Right now all 5,000 high-variance genes get the same ridge penalty, so the few genes that actually relate to response are diluted among genes that don't (sex, stromal or immune genes). This change scales each gene by its mean squared correlation with the 200 z-scored drug responses, raised to a power p. This acts as multi-task relevance weighting shared across drugs, which keeps it fairly stable. The weights are recomputed inside each inner training fold, and p ∈ {0, 1, 2} is chosen by grouped inner CV at the best (γ, η); p=0 gives back the current model exactly.

Everything in the current model is a kernel ridge, so any non-additive or threshold effects on the main shared response axes (general sensitivity, haematopoietic vs solid, and so on) are only captured indirectly. This change adds a small LightGBM model that predicts the top 10 drug-response factor scores (taken from an SVD of the imputed training z-AUC matrix) from the top 50 expression principal components. It maps those predictions back to all 200 drugs, then blends the result with the current prediction using a weight b chosen by grouped inner CV; b=0 gives back the current model exactly.
